title: Genetically Modified Crops
resolution: Resolved: The benefits of genetically modified crops outweigh their harms.
summary: Most U.S. corn, soybeans and cotton are genetically engineered. A major scientific review found them safe to eat, but debates continue over farming practices, weeds, seed ownership and promised benefits.

background.p: Genetically modified (genetically engineered) crops have had genes added or changed to give them traits such as resistance to insects or tolerance of herbicides. They have been grown widely in the United States since the late 1990s, especially corn, soybeans and cotton.

In 2016, a committee of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, chaired by entomologist Fred Gould (who had earlier criticized some GM crops), reviewed hundreds of studies. It found no evidence that genetically engineered crops on the market were riskier to eat than conventional crops, and no evidence that they had reduced plant and insect diversity on farms. It also found no evidence they had sped up the long-term rise in crop yields, said insect-resistant crops had let some farmers spray less insecticide while insects could evolve resistance, and recommended that new crops be reviewed based on their novelty and risk rather than how they were made. Some critics questioned panel members' industry ties.

positions: Supporters point to farm-level studies showing higher yields and less crop loss to pests, especially in developing countries.
The 2016 National Academies review found no evidence that GM traits had sped up the overall rise in U.S. yields.

terms.def: Crops whose DNA has been changed using modern molecular techniques.
Crops that make a protein from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* that kills certain insect pests.
Crops engineered to survive a weed killer, so farmers can spray fields without killing the crop.
Newer methods (such as CRISPR) that make precise changes to a plant's own genes.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: GM crops are safe to eat and have brought real benefits to farmers and the environment.

args.claim: GM foods on the market are as safe to eat as conventional foods.
args.warrant: After decades of study and widespread eating, large scientific reviews have found no added risk, so fears about eating them aren't supported.
args.evidence: National Academies (2016) review; statements by scientific bodies.
args.response: The negative answers that eating safety isn't the main dispute; the harms are in farming practices, weeds and economics.

args.claim: Insect-resistant crops have cut insecticide spraying.
args.warrant: When the plant itself resists certain pests, farmers can spray less, which reduces costs and exposure for workers and wildlife.
args.evidence: National Academies findings on reduced insecticide use for some crops; farm studies of Bt cotton and corn.
args.response: The negative replies that pests are evolving resistance, and herbicide use rose with herbicide-tolerant crops.

args.claim: Genetic engineering can solve problems breeding can't.
args.warrant: Engineering can add traits like virus resistance or extra nutrients faster than conventional breeding, helping farmers facing diseases or nutritional gaps.
args.evidence: Cases such as virus-resistant papaya in Hawaii and nutrient-enhanced crops; reports on gene-edited crops.
args.response: The negative argues that several promised nutritional crops have reached few farmers, and conventional breeding has also improved yields.

args.claim: Farmers choose them because they work.
args.warrant: Farmers pay more for GM seed only if it saves them labor, pesticide or losses; their widespread choice reflects real benefits on the farm.
args.evidence: USDA data on adoption rates; farmer surveys on time and cost savings.
args.response: The negative replies that seed choices narrowed as a few companies came to dominate seed markets, so adoption may reflect limited options.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Even if GM foods are safe to eat, the way these crops are used has brought harms that outweigh the benefits.

args.claim: Herbicide-tolerant crops have helped breed resistant weeds.
args.warrant: Spraying the same weed killer over huge areas year after year selects for weeds that survive it, pushing farmers to stronger chemicals.
args.evidence: Research on glyphosate-resistant weeds; National Academies discussion of resistance; weed-science surveys.
args.response: The affirmative answers that resistance comes from how herbicides are used, not genetic engineering itself, and better rotation fixes it.

args.claim: The promised benefits have been oversold.
args.warrant: If GM crops haven't raised yields faster, the case that they're needed to feed the world is weaker.
args.evidence: National Academies (2016) finding no evidence of faster yield growth in the U.S.
args.response: The affirmative replies that reduced losses to pests and lower spraying are benefits even without faster yield growth.

args.claim: Patents and seed concentration hurt farmers.
args.warrant: Patented seeds can't be saved and replanted, and a few companies control much of the market, raising seed prices and limiting choice.
args.evidence: USDA and antitrust research on seed-industry concentration; seed price data.
args.response: The affirmative answers that hybrid conventional seeds also aren't saved, and patents fund the research that creates new varieties.

args.claim: Unwanted spread can hurt other farmers.
args.warrant: Pollen and seed can drift into organic or non-GM fields, costing those farmers their markets.
args.evidence: Cases of GM traits found in non-GM crops; organic certification rules.
args.response: The affirmative replies that buffer zones and coexistence rules reduce this, and cases are rare.

strawmen.strawman: GMO supporters are just paid by big chemical companies.
strawmen.why: Many independent scientists and reviews support the safety findings; attacking motives skips the evidence.
strawmen.steelman: Large independent reviews find GM foods safe to eat, insect-resistant crops have cut spraying, and engineering can deliver traits breeding can't.

strawmen.strawman: GMO critics think genetically modified food is poison.
strawmen.why: Many critics accept the safety findings and focus on farming practices, weeds and seed markets.
strawmen.steelman: Even if safe to eat, GM crops have encouraged herbicide-resistant weeds, delivered less than promised on yields, and concentrated seed markets.

weak.arg: Without GMOs, the world would starve.
weak.why: The yield evidence doesn't support this; it invites an easy answer.
Major scientific reviews found no evidence of added health risk from eating approved GM foods. It will cost you the round.

aff: What did the National Academies find about yields?
neg: Did the National Academies find GM foods riskier to eat?
Have Bt crops reduced insecticide spraying?
Is herbicide resistance caused by engineering or by how herbicides are used?
